inf-cellulitis.title: Cellulitis
inf-cellulitis.blurb: Two days of spreading warmth and redness over the lower leg, with a poorly demarcated.
inf-cellulitis.summary: Cellulitis presents with two days of spreading warmth and redness over the lower leg, typically with a poorly demarcated, warm, tender erythematous plaque with linear streaking. Clinical diagnosis with marking of the advancing border confirms it, and empiric antibiotic therapy covering streptococci is the initial management.

sections.heading: Overview
paras: Cellulitis describes the clinical picture of two days of spreading warmth and redness over the lower leg produced by dermal and subcutaneous bacterial infection spreading through tissue planes. Sections below follow one conventional sequence — mechanism, presentation, confirmation, management — and each can be read on its own.

Reported frequency varies with the population studied and with the threshold chosen to define a case, so figures quoted in different sources are rarely directly comparable. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that outlining the border with a skin marker turns tomorrow’s exam into an objective test of therapy.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: What drives the picture is dermal and subcutaneous bacterial infection spreading through tissue planes. Tracing the picture back to that single process explains why the individual findings travel together rather than appearing in isolation.

Compensatory responses mask the process early and fail late, which is why the interval between the first abnormality and the first symptom can be long. Understanding this is what makes empiric antibiotic therapy covering streptococci the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation
paras: Two days of spreading warmth and redness over the lower leg is the complaint that brings the patient in, and its evolution over days to weeks is the detail worth pinning down.

Partial or atypical presentations are common enough that the absence of one expected feature should not close the question. A history of two days of spreading warmth and redness over the lower leg in the right context is enough to bring the diagnosis to the front of the differential.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: The sign to look for is a poorly demarcated, warm, tender erythematous plaque with linear streaking; it is more specific than the rest of the examination and is worth eliciting carefully.
A normal examination early in the course is common and does not argue meaningfully against the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paras: The first investigation is clinical diagnosis with marking of the advancing border; ordering it early avoids a sequence of tests that each exclude one possibility.

Testing before the pre-test probability has been thought through produces results that are difficult to act on in either direction. The alternative most often confused with it is infectious mononucleosis, which is compared below.
